title: Segmentation: above-array oxide switches slice each bitline into eight
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation resolves 'long bitline for few sense amps' versus 'short bitline for big signal': row-address-controlled IGZO isolation switches, built in BEOL above the array at zero silicon area, cut each bitline every 64 cells so only the segment holding the active row is connected to the sense amp.
why: Facts 1 and 7: effective bitline capacitance drops ~8x and the transfer ratio rises ~5x, so either sense-amp count falls ~4-8x (periphery ~49% to ~30% of die) or capacitor aspect ratio can relax from ~70:1 to ~20:1.

title: Taking out: periphery made in U.S. mature fabs, bonded to arrays
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out pulls the ~49% periphery off the EUV array wafer: sense amps, decoders, pumps and I/O are made on 28-40 nm logic wafers in existing U.S. fabs and hybrid-bonded face-to-face at ~1 um pitch onto array-only wafers. A national 'periphery foundry' program qualifies one bonding interface that several array suppliers can use.
why: Facts 4 and 7 plus U.S. manufacturability: array die area per bit ~-45%, array wafer masks ~-20-30%, and about half of each DRAM's value-added silicon moves onshore without building an EUV fab.

title: Local quality: few precision sense amps steered to weak columns
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality replaces uniform sense amps: 7 of every 8 are minimum-size latches and 1 of 8 is a large offset-cancelled precision amp. Wafer test maps columns with weak cells or high-offset latches, and a column steering mux routes only those bitlines to the precision amps.
why: Facts 1 and 7: the worst-case tail sets device size for only ~12% of amps, so sense-amp strip area falls ~35% while read margin is kept for the ~1% weak-cell tail.

title: Asymmetry: leak-aware reference skew plus non-leaking-state data encoding
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: cells leak only from '1' toward '0', so the sense reference is shifted toward the '0' side, letting decaying '1's stay readable much longer, while the controller applies a per-64 B invert flag so that at least half the stored bits sit in the non-leaking discharged state that tolerates the reduced margin.
why: Fact 3: refresh interval can roughly double (refresh energy and bandwidth ~-40-50%) and fewer bits are exposed to the retention tail; costs one flag bit per 64 B and a trimmed reference.

title: Merging: wordline driver doubles as analog row-hammer activation counter
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: each sub-wordline driver gets a tiny pumped capacitor that gains a fixed charge packet on every activation and leaks with a ~32 ms time constant; when it crosses a Schmitt threshold the driver flags its two neighbours for targeted refresh. Counting is merged into the device that already sees every activation.
why: Fact 9: deterministic per-row protection at ~1k-activation thresholds for ~2-4% area, instead of 10-20% SRAM/CAM tracking overhead in the controller or die, with no bandwidth spent on blind refresh.

title: Universality: sense amps chain into shift register, deleting column decoders
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: after a row is latched, each sense amp also acts as one stage of a two-phase shift register (two extra transistors couple neighbours), streaming the page out of one edge port. Column decoders, column-select lines and most local I/O wiring disappear; random columns are reached by pipelined skip-shifting.
why: Fact 7: removes column decoders and CSL drivers (~8-12% of die) at the cost of extra latency for far columns; a natural fit for sequential AI tensor streaming.

title: Nesting: sub-wordline drivers built inside the array's vertical-transistor process
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: sub-wordline driver transistors are made as vertical-channel devices in the same pillar and buried-wordline steps as the cells, nested in a dummy-row band inside each mat, so the separate SWD stripes of planar logic transistors and their array-to-periphery boundary rules vanish.
why: Fact 7: SWD stripes are ~8-10% of die; nesting removes ~70% of that area and its extra masks, about a 6% die shrink per node with no lithography change.

title: Anti-weight: switched negative capacitance cancels bitline load during sensing
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight counterbalances the dead weight of bitline capacitance: during the charge-sharing window a switched-capacitor negative-impedance converter (or a thin ferroelectric negative-capacitance layer in the bitline shield dielectric) presents about -0.7 CBL, so the cell sees ~30% of the physical bitline load; it is disconnected before restore to stay stable.
why: Fact 1: transfer ratio up ~3x, so storage capacitance can drop from ~5 fF to ~2 fF (aspect ratio ~30:1) or bitlines can be 3x longer with 3x fewer sense amps.

title: Prior counteraction: data-aware counter-kick cancels bitline coupling before sensing
idea: TRIZ #9 Prior counteraction: a small per-bank row-history cache predicts the neighbouring bitlines' data for the row about to open, and the precharge circuit injects a calibrated counter-charge through dedicated coupling caps so the worst-case bitline-to-bitline coupling during amplification is cancelled in advance.
why: Facts 1 and 8: recovers the ~20-30% of sense margin lost to coupling, allowing open-bitline layouts without twisting or ~25% smaller cell signal.

title: Other way round: column-first activation fires only requested wordline segments
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of row-first (open 8 KB, then pick 64 B), the column address arrives first and is AND-ed with the main wordline at each sub-wordline driver, so only the 1-2 segments and local sense-amp groups under that column fire.
why: Fact 8: overfetch drops from 128x to ~2-4x and random-read energy from ~5.9 pJ toward ~0.3-0.6 pJ per useful bit; fewer opened cells also reduces row-hammer stress per access.

title: Curvature: ring-gate annular transistors make edge-free matched sense amp pairs
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality: the cross-coupled sense-amp transistors are drawn as annular (ring-gate) devices with the drain in the centre, so there is no STI channel edge; edge-related threshold mismatch and narrow-width effects, a major part of sense-amp offset, disappear, and curvilinear masks from multi-beam writers make the rings printable.
why: Facts 1 and 7: sense-amp offset sigma ~-30-40%, so the latch can be ~30% smaller or the cell signal requirement can drop by ~10 mV.

title: Equipotentiality: clamped motionless bitlines with charge-transfer sensing
idea: TRIZ #12 Equipotentiality: each bitline is held at a constant potential by a cascode clamp; the cell's charge flows through the clamp onto a ~0.5 fF sense node, amplified by the capacitance ratio, and restore injects charge back through the same clamp, so the large bitline never swings.
why: Facts 5, 8 and 10: bitline swing energy (~60% of activation energy) drops ~10x and bitline-to-bitline coupling noise nearly vanishes.

title: Dynamics: sense amps switch to two-bit multilevel mode when cool
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: each sense amp adds a second time-staggered latch and a mid-reference so a mat can run either 1-bit robust mode or 2-bit-per-cell multilevel mode; the controller enables multilevel on mats whose thermal sensor and retention telemetry show margin (cool, cold data) and migrates data out when temperature rises.
why: Density: ~1.6-2x bits per cell on cool, cold data, with capacity that flexes with conditions; Fact 1's small charge sets the risk.

title: Excessive action: multi-row activation sums redundant copies in weak mats
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial or excessive action: in mats with weak cells or high temperature the controller writes each bit into 2-4 rows sharing the same bitlines and later opens them together so their charges sum on the bitline, trading capacity for 2-4x signal instead of scrapping the die or raising refresh.
why: Facts 1 and 3: dies with weak tails sell at reduced capacity instead of being scrapped (yield ~+5-15%), and refresh in redundant mode can drop ~4x.

title: Another dimension: stacked CFET sense amp fits a single bitline pitch
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: the cross-coupled latch is built as complementary FETs stacked vertically (nFET pair under pFET pair with shared gates), so each sense amp fits one bitline pitch instead of two to four, letting every bitline of a 4F2 open-bitline array have its own amp.
why: Facts 4 and 7: sense-amp strip area ~-50% and 4F2 vertical-channel cells become usable, since their pitch cannot host today's planar sense amps.

title: Oscillation: bitline voltage tunes ring oscillators, counters compare frequency
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration: after charge sharing, each sense node starves the supply of a tiny ring oscillator; a counter shared by 16 bitlines tallies cycles over 2-5 ns against a reference oscillator, turning a sub-10 mV difference into a digital count with built-in noise averaging, followed by a digital write-back.
why: Facts 1 and 7: frequency-domain sensing tolerates ~3-5x smaller signals and is synthesizable logic with no matched analog pairs, so it shrinks with logic nodes.

title: Periodic action: resonant LC wordline drive recycles boost energy
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: wordlines are driven from a resonant tank formed by an interposer inductor and the selected wordline capacitance, so the ~3 V boost arrives as a half-sine and its charge returns to the tank when the wordline falls, bypassing most of the ~30%-efficient VPP charge pump.
why: Fact 10: wordline/VPP energy ~-60% and charge-pump area in the periphery ~-50%.

title: Skipping: precharge-free rail sensing with auto-zeroed reference sample
idea: TRIZ #21 Skipping: the equalize/precharge phase is skipped; each bitline stays at the rail it was last restored to, a coupling capacitor samples that level, and the sense amp compares the next cell's charge-sharing step against the sample plus a half-signal kick, alternating polarity each cycle.
why: Facts 7 and 8: equalizers and the VBL/2 generator disappear (~5% periphery area), tRP leaves the critical path (~15-20% shorter row cycle) and ~10% activation energy is saved.

title: Blessing in disguise: random sense amp offsets form a reference ladder
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: a bank of 8 tiny unequalized latches per 64 bitlines samples each held bitline voltage in turn; their natural random offsets (sigma ~15 mV), measured once at test, act as a free reference ladder, so the pattern of which latches flip gives 2-3 bits of soft information or multilevel reads with no reference generators.
why: Density and reliability: soft-read information for ECC or 2-bit cells without reference circuitry; mismatch, normally Fact 7's area driver, becomes the resource.

title: Feedback: time-to-resolve margin meter schedules per-row refresh
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: a shared completion detector measures how long each sense amp takes to resolve during refresh; rows whose bits resolve slowly (low remaining charge) are logged in a small per-bank weak-row table and refreshed sooner, while fast-resolving rows stretch their interval to 256 ms or more.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy and bandwidth ~-50-70% because only measured-weak rows get the fast rate, with no pre-test retention profiling.

title: Self-service: refresh bursts double as sense amp offset self-calibration
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: during each refresh burst one sense amp per mat reads an equalized (shorted) bitline pair and the result steps a 4-bit successive-approximation trim register that back-biases or capacitively offsets that amp; over one refresh window every amp re-trims itself, tracking aging and temperature.
why: Facts 1 and 7: effective offset sigma ~3x lower, so cells need ~30% less signal or amps can be minimum-size, and wafer-level trim test time is removed.

title: Phase transition: insulator-metal switch replaces the cross-coupled latch
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transition: a single NbO2 or VO2 threshold-switching element biased just below its insulator-to-metal transition sits on the sense node; the few extra millivolts from a stored '1' tip it abruptly into the metallic state, giving full-swing output from one device instead of a 4-6 transistor latch, and a reset pulse returns it to insulating.
why: Fact 7: sense-amp area could fall ~4x and fit the bitline pitch, and the abrupt gain tolerates smaller storage charge; threshold variability and thermal crosstalk are the risks.

title: Beforehand cushioning: weak-written sentinel rows trigger early mat refresh
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: each mat reserves two sentinel rows that are written at only ~70% of the array voltage, making them deliberately weaker than any data row; they are read on every refresh pass, and the first sentinel failure raises that mat's refresh rate before real data is at risk.
why: Fact 3: lets the default refresh interval be set aggressively (~2x longer) with a built-in early warning, so ~30-40% of refresh energy is saved without per-die retention testing.

title: Another dimension: 512-tier vertical charge-coupled strings with one sense node
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: bits are charge packets in potential wells along a vertical oxide-semiconductor channel gated by 512 stacked wordline plates, a one-hole 3D-NAND-like process with no capacitor and no per-bit transistor. Reads clock the packets CCD-style down the pillar into one floating-diffusion sense node under the array, which regenerates them and re-injects them at the top, so refresh is just recirculation.
why: 100x path: NAND-like cost (~$0.05-0.15/GB) because periphery is one sense node per 512 bits, no EUV and few masks per tier; trade-offs: serial 10-50 us page access, and charge-transfer inefficiency and dark current cap string length, so a small DRAM cache must front it. Attacks Facts 1, 2, 4 and 7.

title: Taking out: transistor-free array dies time-share one CMOS reader die
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: array dies hold only capacitor cells, oxide-TFT access devices and a TFT 1024:1 bitline multiplexer, built with ~10 masks on depreciated 65-90 nm lines; 16 such dies stack on one 28 nm CMOS reader die whose sense amps, decoders and I/O serve every die through vertical global bitlines, one die active at a time.
why: 100x path: no front-end CMOS on 15/16 of the silicon (~3x), mature tools (~4x), periphery amortized 16x (~2x) and cheap stacking (~4x); trade-offs: ~1/16 bandwidth per stack, ~us row cycle and thermal limits. Attacks Facts 4 and 7 and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Excessive action: 256-tier vertical bitline read by chopper auto-zero amplifier
idea: TRIZ #16 Excessive action: one vertical bitline is deliberately overloaded with 256 tiers of planar ~1 fF thin-film capacitor cells (bitline ~300 fF, signal ~1.5 mV) and read by a chopper-stabilized, auto-zeroed, correlated-double-sampling amplifier under the array that integrates for ~1 us, so one amplifier serves 256 stacked cells.
why: 100x path: no high-aspect-ratio capacitor module, no EUV, periphery ~2% of die and BEOL-repeatable tiers; trade-offs: microsecond reads, kT/C noise holds SNR near ~10 so cells must stay at ~1 fF or more, and higher sense energy. Attacks Facts 1, 2 and 7.

title: Periodic action: lock-in readout of varactor cells, no destructive read
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: each storage element is a floating MOS varactor whose small-signal capacitance depends on its stored charge (accumulation versus depletion); a ~10 MHz small excitation on the wordline and a lock-in demodulator shared by 256 bitlines read that capacitance without moving the stored charge, so reads are non-destructive.
why: 100x path: deletes restore/write-back circuits and per-bitline sense amps (256:1 sharing) and allows planar cells stacked in 8+ BEOL tiers on mature or display-class lines; trade-offs: ~1 us reads and lower density per tier. Also removes Fact 8's destructive read.

title: Composite: silicon sense chiplets mass-transferred onto glass DRAM panels
idea: TRIZ #40 Composite: large glass panels carry stacked oxide-TFT DRAM tiers, while all precision sensing lives in 50x50 um silicon sense chiplets placed every few millimetres by micro-LED-style mass transfer (millions per hour) and wired by panel redistribution layers; glass does storage, silicon does amplification.
why: 100x path: panel processing costs ~$100-300/m2 versus ~$100k/m2 for EUV DRAM wafers, so with ~0.3 um panel nanoimprint and 16-32 TFT tiers it aims at ~$0.1-0.5/GB; trade-offs: bulky modules, ~us latency and higher energy. Speculative because panel lithography must improve ~5x. Attacks Facts 4 and 7.

title: Asymmetry: per-bitline read inverters, one slow shared write scanner
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: for read-mostly AI weights and KV-cache, a 2T oxide gain cell is read non-destructively by a single minimum-size inverter per bitline (no latch, no reference, no restore), while writes go through one high-voltage scanning write driver per 64k cells at ~10 us per row.
why: 100x path: read periphery ~10x smaller, write drivers amortized ~1000x, cells stacked 8+ BEOL tiers on mature nodes; trade-offs: writes 100-1000x slower, so it is unsuitable for write-heavy data. Attacks Facts 4 and 7.

title: Discarding and recovering: JEDEC managed-DRAM class without on-die repair
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: a new JEDEC 'managed DRAM' class removes laser/e-fuse repair banks, redundancy muxes and most wafer-sort retention testing from the die; the host discovers bad rows and columns at boot with a BIST march, discards them and recovers capacity from 5-10% over-provisioning, as NAND does with bad blocks.
why: 100x enabler: repair periphery (~5% of die) and test (~10-15% of cost) go away, and arrays can be built in low-cost, defect-tolerant processes that are unshippable today; trade-offs: capacity varies per part and boot-time mapping is required.

title: Thermal expansion: latching bimorph nano-relays as zero-leakage wordline decoders
idea: TRIZ #37 Thermal expansion: wordline decoders are built from bistable electrothermal bimorph nano-relays patterned in BEOL metal and oxide layers above the array, with no transistors; a heat pulse flexes a relay into contact where it latches mechanically, routing ~3 V wordline drive with zero off-state leakage.
why: 100x path: decoders move out of front-end silicon into ~4 cheap metal masks at 90 nm-class pitch, enabling transistor-free periphery over stacked arrays; trade-offs: ~0.1-1 us switching and relay wear (~1e9-1e12 cycles) limits activations per row. Attacks Facts 7 and 10.

title: Parameter change: 77 K operation lets junk polysilicon transistors stack 64-high
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change: memory sleds run immersed at 77 K, where leakage of cheap low-temperature polysilicon access transistors falls by ~1e6 and kT/C noise by ~4x, so 64 BEOL tiers of poly-Si 1T1C cells with planar ~2 fF capacitors hold data for minutes and are read by small low-offset cryo-CMOS sense amps under the array.
why: 100x path: 64 cheap tiers on a 40 nm logic base (~30x more bits per dollar of area), refresh periphery deleted, sense amps ~2x smaller; trade-offs: liquid-nitrogen infrastructure and ~10 W of cooling per W dissipated, so it suits rack-scale memory pools. Attacks Facts 2, 3 and 4.

title: Copying: optical readout of stacked electro-optic charge films
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying replaces per-bit silicon sensing with an optical copy: bits are charge in a transistor-free photoconductor/electro-optic film stack (like optically addressed light modulators), written by a micro-LED projector and read by a CMOS image sensor that selects one of 32 films through wavelength-selective layers; refresh is re-projecting the captured image.
why: 100x path: the storage films cost cents per m2 and one image sensor plus micro-LED array serves 32 films and millions of bits per frame; trade-offs: 1-10 us frame latency, optical volume, ms retention requiring constant re-copy, and interlayer crosstalk. Attacks Facts 4 and 7.

title: Local quality: graded-threshold tiers replace the 3D staircase decoder
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: each tier of a 3D stack is deposited with its own in-situ doping so its select-transistor pair (one n-type, one p-type in series) has thresholds stepped ~150 mV per tier, forming a voltage window; a single vertical gate rod driven by one precision DAC level opens exactly one tier, with no staircase contact etch.
why: 100x path: deletes the staircase (~10-20% of 3D die area and dozens of trim/etch steps) so tiers can scale cheaply; trade-offs: threshold control limits each window band to ~16-32 tiers, and selection is slower. Attacks Facts 2, 4 and 7.

title: Merging: dual-gate access devices decode 1024 rows with 64 drivers
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging moves the last decode stage into the cells: each oxide-TFT access device has a bottom gate tied to a group plate (32 groups) and a top gate tied to an in-group line strapped across groups (32 lines), and conducts only when both are high, so 1024 wordlines need 64 drivers instead of 1024 sub-wordline drivers.
why: 100x path: wordline-driver area falls ~16x and the remaining periphery fits under one tier, making 8-16 stacked TFT tiers on a mature logic base viable; trade-offs: half-selected cells need a strong dual-gate threshold shift and see more disturb, and wordline RC is slower. Attacks Fact 7.

title: Intermediary: threshold-switch selector capacitor crossbar with edge-only periphery
idea: TRIZ #24 Intermediary: an ovonic threshold switch in series with each capacitor (1S1C) lets the capacitor charge or discharge only when the full row-column voltage exceeds the switch threshold, while half-selected cells stay isolated; arrays become transistor-free crossbars stacked 8 decks high in BEOL, with decoders and sense amps only at array edges.
why: 100x path: zero transistors in the array, ~2 masks per deck and periphery amortized over 8 decks on a mature-node base; trade-offs: sub-threshold selector leakage limits retention to ~ms (frequent refresh), selector endurance ~1e10-1e12 and higher read energy. Attacks Facts 2 and 4.

title: Blessing in disguise: Geiger-mode avalanche bitline sensing of 100-electron cells
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise turns breakdown, normally a failure, into gain: each bitline segment ends in a SPAD-like junction biased just above avalanche breakdown, which a stored packet of ~100 electrons triggers into a full-swing self-quenched pulse, so storage nodes need only ~0.02 fF and can be plain planar diffusions.
why: 100x path: deletes the capacitor module (Fact 1) and allows near-4F2 planar or stacked cells on mature nodes; trade-offs: dark counts and afterpulsing need repeat reads and strong ECC, ~10-100 ns quench recovery and higher sense voltage. Attacks Facts 1, 2 and 4.

title: Hydraulics: electrolyte-gated printed sense transistors on roll-to-roll film
idea: TRIZ #29 Pneumatics and hydraulics: the solid gate dielectric of the sense and decode circuits is replaced by a printed ion-gel electrolyte whose double-layer capacitance (~10 uF/cm2) gives high transconductance below 1 V, so inkjet- or gravure-printed oxide transistors at 5-10 um can still amplify millivolt bitline signals.
why: 100x path: periphery is printed on film at ~$1-10/m2 with no vacuum fab, pairing with nanoimprinted array films; trade-offs: ionic response of ~1-10 us, temperature sensitivity and large area. Attacks capital intensity (Fact 4) and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Curvature: wound film memory roll with edge-metallized bitline contacts
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality: like a film capacitor, a 5 um polymer strip carrying nanoimprinted oxide-TFT DRAM arrays is wound into a 1000-turn cylinder; bitlines of every turn run to one edge, where sprayed and laser-patterned end-cap metallization connects them to a CMOS reader disk, so all periphery sits on the circular end face.
why: 100x path: roll-to-roll nanoimprint at ~0.5 um aims at ~80 GB/m2 per layer for ~$5-10/m2 (~$0.1/GB), with the reader disk amortized over 1000 turns; trade-offs: us-ms access, retention needs very low-leakage TFTs and end-cap registration is unproven. Attacks Facts 4 and 7.

title: Continuity: rolling-scan drum memory needs only a shift-register row scanner
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: like a display gate driver, a shift register sweeps every row in order, sensing and restoring each (so refresh is the scan itself) and presenting each row to a page buffer as it passes; requests wait for their row to come around, removing row address decoders, refresh logic and most control.
why: 100x path: row periphery shrinks to a TFT gate-driver-on-array strip (~1-2% of area) buildable on glass or BEOL lines and repeatable in stacked tiers; trade-offs: average latency is half a scan (~5-30 us), so it suits streaming and batched AI tensors. Attacks Facts 3 and 7.

title: Homogeneity: n-type-only oxide periphery built with the array masks
idea: TRIZ #33 Homogeneity: every periphery circuit uses the same n-type IGZO TFT as the array, with bootstrapped dynamic logic, pseudo-differential charge-transfer sense amps and capacitive level shifters, so the whole chip, array plus periphery, needs ~8-10 masks with no wells or implants and can be repeated tier after tier.
why: 100x path: ~8x fewer masks than 60-80-mask DRAM, no EUV, and periphery repeated in each stacked tier keeps tiers independent and testable; trade-offs: ~10x slower periphery (us-class) and higher dynamic power. Attacks Facts 4 and 7 and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Prior action: commodity periphery base wafers sold for array build-up
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: a merchant foundry pre-manufactures standardized periphery base wafers (sense amps, decoders, pumps and I/O on a fixed grid at 40 nm) in very high volume, and low-capex array companies add only BEOL memory tiers on top, as with gate arrays and structured ASICs.
why: 100x path: array entrants skip ~$15B front-end fabs and periphery design cost, base wafers aim at <$1500 at volume, and BEOL tier lines cost ~$0.5-1B; trade-offs: a fixed periphery limits array flexibility. Attacks capital intensity (Fact 4) and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Beforehand cushioning: NAND-grade LDPC lets sense amps run at 1e-3 errors
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: a 4 KB-codeword LDPC decoder with soft-read support in the base die absorbs raw bit error rates up to ~1e-3, so sense amps can be minimum-size latches with large offset, cells ~2x smaller, and 2-bit multilevel storage practical.
why: 100x path: ~2x periphery shrink, ~2x cell shrink and ~2x bits per cell compound with stacking; trade-offs: ~0.5-2 us decode latency, 4 KB access granularity and ~10% parity overhead. Attacks Facts 1 and 7.

title: Skipping: read-once scratch memory omits restore and refresh circuits
idea: TRIZ #21 Skipping: for streaming activations and KV-cache spills written once and read once within milliseconds, the cell is read destructively and restore and refresh are skipped entirely; the periphery loses write-back drivers, refresh counters and the restore VPP budget, and cells need only ~5 ms retention, so a ~0.5 fF planar capacitor is enough.
why: 100x path: no high-aspect-ratio capacitor, periphery ~30% smaller and BEOL-stackable planar cells on mature nodes; trade-offs: each datum is consumed by its read (re-reads need a host copy) and data expires after milliseconds. Attacks Facts 1, 3 and 8.

title: Self-service: read-write-read self-reference removes matched sense amp pairs
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: each read samples the bitline after charge sharing, writes a known '1', shares again and samples a second time, comparing the cell with itself on one capacitor pair; device mismatch, reference bitlines and dummy cells cancel, so sloppy TFT or 180 nm transistors can serve as the sense amp.
why: 100x path: sensing works with ~100 mV-offset cheap devices and single-ended bitlines on mature or TFT lines; trade-offs: ~3x longer read cycle and an extra write per read (energy and disturb). Attacks Facts 4 and 7.

title: Feedback: shared sigma-delta loops read three bits per cell
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: after charge sharing each bitline holds its voltage on its own capacitance while one 1-bit sigma-delta modulator per 128 bitlines visits them in turn, feeding back charge packets until balanced, resolving 8 charge levels (3 bits) per planar cell in ~2 us instead of a binary latch per bitline.
why: 100x path: 3x bits per cell and 128x fewer sensing circuits, compounded with stacked mature-node tiers; trade-offs: microsecond reads, cells must hold ~8x finer charge levels so leakage must be very low (oxide TFTs), and refresh must rewrite multilevel values. Attacks Facts 1 and 7.
